newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa commission favours source based tax.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa commission favours source based tax.

text.p: The Commission of Inquiry into South Africa's tax structure has recommended that active income should continue to be taxed on a source basis, while passive income should be taxed on a worldwide basis.

In its fifth interim report released on Friday, the commission said it favoured the German and U.K. approaches to anti-avoidance measures aimed at dealing with the country's growing re-entry into the global economy and the removal of exchange controls.

It said the current source system helped encourage domestic or foreign businesses to base holding companies, headquarter companies and finance companies in South Africa for investment and trade into Africa, and in particular southern Africa.
"Preserving and even extending it would benefit the economy directly and help South Africa acquit itself of its regional developmental responsibilities," it said.
Maintaining the source principle on active -- salary or trading -- income provided the kind of tax neutrality that was good in principle and allowed the country to participate in the global economy.
It said that in a broad sense, taxing passive income -- income earned on assets -- was the same as extending the current source provisions to include all forms of passive income.
"That means that South African residents, corporate or individual, should pay South African tax on their passive income, irrespective of the source of such income," the report said.
This measure would protect the tax base from possible erosion when exchange controls were lifted.

"Since South Africa already applies a fair measure of worldwide taxation of passive income, as well as commensurate anti-avoidance measures in that context, some administrative and legal infrastructure already exists.
"Therefore, expanding it need not add materially to complexity," it said.
On anti-avoidance measures, the commission said it strongly recommended the German and British approaches through a manageable balance between scope and pragmatism.
Over-elaborate anti-avoidance measures, such as those in the U.S. and Australia, were often less effective than administratively feasible ones.
Such measures could seriously inhibit international trade and investment, it said.

"The commission emphasises that the need for these measures, and the complexity that comes with them, is not the result of its recommendations as such, but of South Africa's growing re-entry into the global economy, espcially once exchange controls are relaxed."

As South Africans participated increasingly in the global economy, the country would require measures similar to any other control-free system, irrespective of whether it was primarily residence or source based, it added.
